understand.concept: A dictionary value can itself be a dictionary. Access nested data one key at a time, check each level when keys may be absent, and avoid assuming that every record has an identical shape.
understand.whyItMatters: Nested Dictionaries is useful when a program needs to organize, inspect or transform related data reliably.
understand.analogy: A dictionary is like a labeled set of drawers: a key identifies the drawer that contains a value.
understand.analogyLimit: A dictionary key is not a physical drawer; keys must be hashable and lookup follows Python's mapping rules.

explain.narrative:
## Nested Dictionaries

A dictionary value can itself be a dictionary. Access nested data one key at a time, check each level when keys may be absent, and avoid assuming that every record has an identical shape.

## Choosing an operation

Read the example code and check whether the operation mutates the object, returns a new value, or may raise an exception. Use membership tests and defaults where input may be missing.

## Practical reasoning

The five examples progress from basic use to a small real-world pattern. Compare each expected output with the code before changing it.

examples.title:
people = {'p1': {'name': 'Asha'}, 'p2': {'name': 'Ravi'}}
print(people['p2']['name'])
examples.expectedOutput: The first key selects a record; the second selects a field.

examples.title:
store = {'stock': {'pens': 12, 'books': 5}}
print(store['stock']['pens'])
examples.expectedOutput: Chained indexing follows the nested mapping structure.
Supplying an empty dictionary default allows a second safe get.
The inner dictionary is mutable and can be updated through its parent.
items exposes each team and its nested details mapping.
